claim: Explanted marginal zones (MZs) generate tensile convergence forces up to 1.5 μN during gastrulation.
source: We show that explanted MZs generate tensile convergence forces up to 1.5 μN during gastrulation and over 4 μN thereafter.
evidence: The abstract directly states measured force values from explanted MZs during gastrulation.

claim: Explanted marginal zones generate tensile convergence forces over 4 μN after gastrulation.
source: We show that explanted MZs generate tensile convergence forces up to 1.5 μN during gastrulation and over 4 μN thereafter.
evidence: The abstract directly states measured force values from explanted MZs after gastrulation.

claim: Convergent thickening (CT) generates forces until the midgastrula stage.
source: These forces are generated by convergent thickening (CT) until the midgastrula and increasingly by convergent extension (CE) thereafter.
evidence: The abstract states the temporal pattern of force generation by CT.

claim: Convergent extension (CE) increasingly generates forces after the midgastrula stage.
source: These forces are generated by convergent thickening (CT) until the midgastrula and increasingly by convergent extension (CE) thereafter.
evidence: The abstract states the temporal pattern of force generation by CE.

claim: Explants from ventralized embryos produce up to 2 μN of tensile force.
source: Explants from ventralized embryos, which lack tissues expressing CE but close their blastopores, produce up to 2 μN of tensile force, showing that CT alone generates forces sufficient to close the blastopore.
evidence: The abstract directly states measured force values from ventralized embryo explants.

claim: Ventralized embryos lack tissues expressing convergent extension (CE).
source: Explants from ventralized embryos, which lack tissues expressing CE but close their blastopores, produce up to 2 μN of tensile force, showing that CT alone generates forces sufficient to close the blastopore.
evidence: The abstract states that ventralized embryos lack CE-expressing tissues.

claim: Ventralized embryos close their blastopores.
source: Explants from ventralized embryos, which lack tissues expressing CE but close their blastopores, produce up to 2 μN of tensile force, showing that CT alone generates forces sufficient to close the blastopore.
evidence: The abstract states that ventralized embryos close their blastopores despite lacking CE.

claim: Convergent thickening (CT) alone generates forces sufficient to close the blastopore.
source: Explants from ventralized embryos, which lack tissues expressing CE but close their blastopores, produce up to 2 μN of tensile force, showing that CT alone generates forces sufficient to close the blastopore.
evidence: The abstract concludes that CT alone can generate sufficient force for blastopore closure based on ventralized embryo data.

claim: Mesodermal tissues stiffen around the onset of neurulation.
source: Uniaxial tensile stress relaxation assays show stiffening of mesodermal and ectodermal tissues around the onset of neurulation, potentially enhancing long-range transmission of convergence forces.
evidence: The abstract states that stress relaxation assays demonstrate tissue stiffening at neurulation.

claim: Ectodermal tissues stiffen around the onset of neurulation.
source: Uniaxial tensile stress relaxation assays show stiffening of mesodermal and ectodermal tissues around the onset of neurulation, potentially enhancing long-range transmission of convergence forces.
evidence: The abstract states that stress relaxation assays demonstrate tissue stiffening at neurulation.

claim: Tissue stiffening around neurulation potentially enhances long-range transmission of convergence forces.
source: Uniaxial tensile stress relaxation assays show stiffening of mesodermal and ectodermal tissues around the onset of neurulation, potentially enhancing long-range transmission of convergence forces.
evidence: The abstract speculates about the functional consequence of tissue stiffening.

claim: Blastopore closure during gastrulation of anamniotes depends on circumblastoporal convergence forces generated by the marginal zone (MZ).
source: Indirect evidence suggests that blastopore closure during gastrulation of anamniotes, including amphibians such as Xenopus laevis, depends on circumblastoporal convergence forces generated by the marginal zone (MZ), but direct evidence is lacking.
evidence: The introduction states that indirect evidence suggests this mechanism, citing the lack of direct evidence.

claim: Direct evidence for circumblastoporal convergence forces driving blastopore closure was lacking prior to this study.
source: Indirect evidence suggests that blastopore closure during gastrulation of anamniotes, including amphibians such as Xenopus laevis, depends on circumblastoporal convergence forces generated by the marginal zone (MZ), but direct evidence is lacking.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states that direct evidence was lacking.

claim: Breaking the continuity of the IMZ transverse to the axis of its convergence results in catastrophic failure of normal involution and blastopore closure.
source: The role of circumblastoporal tensile force in amphibian blastopore closure was inferred from the fact that breaking the continuity of the IMZ transverse to the axis of its convergence, and putative tensile force, results in catastrophic failure of normal involution and blastopore closure (Schechtman, 1942; Keller, 1981, 1984); reviewed in Keller et al., 2003).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies showing that cutting the IMZ disrupts blastopore closure.

claim: Convergent extension (CE) is an autonomous force-producing process of the IMZ.
source: The source of this tensile force was thought to be Convergent Extension (CE), an autonomous force-producing process of the IMZ in which its cells express a mediolaterally polarized cell motility, resulting in the intercalation of cells along the mediolateral axis to produce a narrower, longer array, which generates a primary convergence force, and in turn, an extension force (Moore, 1994; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction describes CE as an autonomous force-producing process based on cited literature.

claim: In convergent extension, cells express mediolaterally polarized cell motility resulting in cell intercalation along the mediolateral axis.
source: The source of this tensile force was thought to be Convergent Extension (CE), an autonomous force-producing process of the IMZ in which its cells express a mediolaterally polarized cell motility, resulting in the intercalation of cells along the mediolateral axis to produce a narrower, longer array, which generates a primary convergence force, and in turn, an extension force (Moore, 1994; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction describes the cellular mechanism of CE based on cited literature.

claim: Convergent extension produces a narrower, longer array of cells.
source: The source of this tensile force was thought to be Convergent Extension (CE), an autonomous force-producing process of the IMZ in which its cells express a mediolaterally polarized cell motility, resulting in the intercalation of cells along the mediolateral axis to produce a narrower, longer array, which generates a primary convergence force, and in turn, an extension force (Moore, 1994; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction describes the morphological outcome of CE based on cited literature.

claim: Convergent extension generates a primary convergence force and an extension force.
source: The source of this tensile force was thought to be Convergent Extension (CE), an autonomous force-producing process of the IMZ in which its cells express a mediolaterally polarized cell motility, resulting in the intercalation of cells along the mediolateral axis to produce a narrower, longer array, which generates a primary convergence force, and in turn, an extension force (Moore, 1994; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction describes the forces generated by CE based on cited literature.

claim: Disrupting mediolaterally polarized cell motility by perturbation of the planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway blocks convergence in embryos and explants.
source: Disrupting this mediolaterally polarized cell motility (called 'mediolateral intercalation behavior', MIB) by perturbation of the planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway, blocks convergence in embryos and explants (Djiane et al., 2000; Tada and Smith, 2000; Wallingford et al., 2000; Habas et al., 2001; Goto and Keller, 2002; Habas et al., 2003; Ewald et al., 2004).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies showing that PCP pathway disruption blocks convergence.

claim: Feroze et al., 2015 measured a convergence force of ~0.5 μN at the blastopore lip of Xenopus embryos.
source: Finally, Feroze et al., 2015 measured a convergence force of ~0.5 μN at the blastopore lip of Xenopus embryos, and Zhou et al. (2015) measured the extension force after blastorpore closure.
evidence: The introduction cites a specific force measurement from a previous study.

claim: Zhou et al. (2015) measured the extension force after blastopore closure.
source: Finally, Feroze et al., 2015 measured a convergence force of ~0.5 μN at the blastopore lip of Xenopus embryos, and Zhou et al. (2015) measured the extension force after blastorpore closure.
evidence: The introduction cites a force measurement from a previous study.

claim: Convergent thickening (CT) was originally defined in explants of the ventral IMZ of Xenopus as an active, radial thickening that results in decreasing its planar dimension.
source: CT was originally defined in explants of the ventral IMZ of Xenopus as an active, radial thickening, perpendicular to the embryonic surface or planar dimension of the tissue, the IMZ in this case, that results in decreasing its planar dimension (convergence), and it was thought to occur only ventrally (Keller and Danilchik, 1988).
evidence: The introduction cites the original definition of CT from a previous study.

claim: Convergent thickening was originally thought to occur only ventrally in Xenopus.
source: CT was originally defined in explants of the ventral IMZ of Xenopus as an active, radial thickening, perpendicular to the embryonic surface or planar dimension of the tissue, the IMZ in this case, that results in decreasing its planar dimension (convergence), and it was thought to occur only ventrally (Keller and Danilchik, 1988).
evidence: The introduction cites the original understanding of CT's spatial distribution.

claim: Convergent thickening occurs throughout the pre-involution IMZ, not just ventrally.
source: Recently, we found that CT occurs throughout the pre-involution IMZ, not just ventrally, and that the cells expressing CT undergo a transition to express CE at involution (Shook et al., 2018) (see Figure 1).
evidence: The introduction cites recent work showing CT occurs throughout the IMZ.

claim: Cells expressing convergent thickening undergo a transition to express convergent extension at involution.
source: Recently, we found that CT occurs throughout the pre-involution IMZ, not just ventrally, and that the cells expressing CT undergo a transition to express CE at involution (Shook et al., 2018) (see Figure 1).
evidence: The introduction cites recent work showing the CT to CE transition.

claim: The mechanism of convergent thickening involves chemotactic polarization of movement.
source: The mechanism involves chemotactic polarization of movement (Szabó et al., 2016), integrin-fibronectin signaling (Marsden and DeSimone, 2001), and boundary capture (Keller, 1980; Szabó et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites studies describing the mechanism of CT.

claim: The mechanism of convergent thickening involves integrin-fibronectin signaling.
source: The mechanism involves chemotactic polarization of movement (Szabó et al., 2016), integrin-fibronectin signaling (Marsden and DeSimone, 2001), and boundary capture (Keller, 1980; Szabó et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites studies describing the mechanism of CT.

claim: The mechanism of convergent thickening involves boundary capture.
source: The mechanism involves chemotactic polarization of movement (Szabó et al., 2016), integrin-fibronectin signaling (Marsden and DeSimone, 2001), and boundary capture (Keller, 1980; Szabó et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites studies describing the mechanism of CT.

claim: During radial intercalation, cells enter the surface plane of the tissue, whereas in convergent thickening cells leave the surface of the tissue.
source: During radial intercalation (often resulting in epiboly) cells enter the surface plane of the tissue, whereas CT is the reverse in that cells leave the surface of the tissue, minimizing tissue surface area, resulting in thickening and convergence of the tissue.
evidence: The introduction contrasts the cellular behavior in radial intercalation versus CT.

claim: Radial intercalation depends on polarized cell behaviors.
source: Another major difference between RI and CT is that, like MIB, RI depends on polarized cell behaviors (Ossipova et al., 2015), whereas our understanding of CT is that the underlying surface tension based mechanism does not require a polarized cell behavior, only motility to maximize high-affinity cell-cell contacts (Shook et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites a study showing RI depends on polarized cell behaviors.

claim: Convergent thickening does not require a polarized cell behavior, only motility to maximize high-affinity cell-cell contacts.
source: Another major difference between RI and CT is that, like MIB, RI depends on polarized cell behaviors (Ossipova et al., 2015), whereas our understanding of CT is that the underlying surface tension based mechanism does not require a polarized cell behavior, only motility to maximize high-affinity cell-cell contacts (Shook et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites a study describing the mechanism of CT.

claim: Convergent thickening occurs throughout the IMZ as gastrulation begins.
source: In our working model, CT (Figure 1A, white symbols) occurs throughout the IMZ as gastrulation begins and decreases the circumference of the IMZ symmetrically from all sides, which tends to push it toward the blastoporal lip and contributes to blastopore closure by advancing the blastoporal lips across the vegetal endoderm (Figure 1A, green arrows, VE; Video 1, left embryo).
evidence: The introduction describes the working model with reference to Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Convergent thickening decreases the circumference of the IMZ symmetrically from all sides.
source: In our working model, CT (Figure 1A, white symbols) occurs throughout the IMZ as gastrulation begins and decreases the circumference of the IMZ symmetrically from all sides, which tends to push it toward the blastoporal lip and contributes to blastopore closure by advancing the blastoporal lips across the vegetal endoderm (Figure 1A, green arrows, VE; Video 1, left embryo).
evidence: The introduction describes the working model with reference to Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Convergent thickening contributes to blastopore closure by advancing the blastoporal lips across the vegetal endoderm.
source: In our working model, CT (Figure 1A, white symbols) occurs throughout the IMZ as gastrulation begins and decreases the circumference of the IMZ symmetrically from all sides, which tends to push it toward the blastoporal lip and contributes to blastopore closure by advancing the blastoporal lips across the vegetal endoderm (Figure 1A, green arrows, VE; Video 1, left embryo).
evidence: The introduction describes the working model with reference to Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Early involuting cells of the presumptive head, heart and lateroventral mesoderm transition to migrating directionally across the blastocoel roof toward the animal pole after involution.
source: The early involuting cells of the presumptive head, heart and lateroventral mesoderm (Figure 1A,B, orange), which expressed CT in the preinvolution IMZ, transition to migrating directionally across the blastocoel roof toward the animal pole after involution (Figure 1B, gray arrows, dorsal cutaway) (Winklbauer and Nagel, 1991).
evidence: The introduction describes cell behavior with reference to Figure 1 and cites a previous study.

claim: Later-involuting presumptive notochordal and somitic mesodermal cells transition on involution to expressing mediolateral intercalation behavior (MIB) and thus convergent extension (CE).
source: In contrast, the following, later-involuting presumptive notochordal and somitic mesodermal cells (Figure 1A,B, magenta and red, respectively), which also expressed CT in the preinvolution IMZ, transition on involution to expressing MIB, and thus CE (Figure 1C, enlargement of 1B, MIB – aligned, black, fusiform cells; CE- green/blue arrows symbol).
evidence: The introduction describes cell behavior with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Expression of mediolateral intercalation behavior (MIB) is progressive, beginning anteriorly at the midgastrula (stage 10.5) with the formation of the Vegetal Alignment Zone (VAZ).
source: Expression of MIB is progressive, beginning anteriorly at the midgastrula (stage 10.5) with the formation of an arc of intercalating cells just inside the dorsal blastopore, called the 'Vegetal Alignment Zone' (Figure 1C, VAZ).
evidence: The introduction describes the progressive expression of MIB with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The Vegetal Alignment Zone (VAZ) spans the dorsal aspect of the blastopore and is anchored at both ends to the vegetal endoderm near the bottle cells.
source: The VAZ spans the dorsal aspect of the blastopore and is anchored at both ends to the vegetal endoderm near the bottle cells (Figure 1C, asterisks indicating anchorage point, VE, BCs,).
evidence: The introduction describes the VAZ structure with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Preinvolution IMZ cells continue to express convergent thickening and aid in blastopore closure throughout gastrulation.
source: As preinvolution IMZ cells continue to express CT and aid in blastopore closure throughout gastrulation (Figure 1D), MIB progresses posteriorly from its anterior origin in the VAZ.
evidence: The introduction describes the continued expression of CT with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Mediolateral intercalation behavior (MIB) progresses posteriorly from its anterior origin in the Vegetal Alignment Zone (VAZ).
source: As preinvolution IMZ cells continue to express CT and aid in blastopore closure throughout gastrulation (Figure 1D), MIB progresses posteriorly from its anterior origin in the VAZ.
evidence: The introduction describes the progression of MIB with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The posterior progressivity of expression of mediolateral intercalation behavior/convergent extension results in an increasingly anisotropic blastoporal closure from stage 10.5 (midgastrula) onward.
source: The posterior progressivity of expression of MIB/CE results in an increasingly anisotropic blastoporal closure from St. 10.5 (midgastrula) onward, with the dorsal/dorsolateral sides closing over the vegetal endoderm faster than the ventral/ventrolateral sides (green arrows, Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The introduction describes the anisotropic blastopore closure with reference to Figure 1D,E.

claim: The dorsal/dorsolateral sides of the blastopore close over the vegetal endoderm faster than the ventral/ventrolateral sides from stage 10.5 onward.
source: The posterior progressivity of expression of MIB/CE results in an increasingly anisotropic blastoporal closure from St. 10.5 (midgastrula) onward, with the dorsal/dorsolateral sides closing over the vegetal endoderm faster than the ventral/ventrolateral sides (green arrows, Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The introduction describes the differential closure rates with reference to Figure 1D,E.

claim: Giant sandwich explants reproduce the major movements described in embryos, excepting involution.
source: To assay circumblastoporal tensile forces, we use 'giant sandwich explants' consisting of the entire IMZ plus posterior ectodermal and neural tissues (Figure 1G). These explants reproduce the major movements described above in embryos, excepting involution (Video 2).
evidence: The introduction describes the explant system with reference to Figure 1G and Video 2.

claim: Convergent thickening occurs early and symmetrically across the entire mediolateral extent of the IMZ in giant sandwich explants, beginning at the onset of gastrulation.
source: CT occurs early and symmetrically across the entire mediolateral extent of the IMZ, beginning at the onset of gastrulation, and produces a progressive thickening and convergence of the IMZ (Figure 1G–H, white symbols; Video 2) (Shook et al., 2018), a convergence that we believe acts as a preloading force that pushes the IMZ toward the blastoporal lip and tends to close the blastopore in embryos as described above.
evidence: The introduction describes CT in explants with reference to Figure 1G-H, Video 2, and cites a previous study.

claim: Convergent thickening produces a progressive thickening and convergence of the IMZ in giant sandwich explants.
source: CT occurs early and symmetrically across the entire mediolateral extent of the IMZ, beginning at the onset of gastrulation, and produces a progressive thickening and convergence of the IMZ (Figure 1G–H, white symbols; Video 2) (Shook et al., 2018), a convergence that we believe acts as a preloading force that pushes the IMZ toward the blastoporal lip and tends to close the blastopore in embryos as described above.
evidence: The introduction describes CT in explants with reference to Figure 1G-H, Video 2, and cites a previous study.

claim: In explants, IMZ cells progressively stop expressing convergent thickening and express postinvolution behaviors, including mediolateral intercalation behavior-driven cell intercalation, beginning at the midgastrula stage.
source: In explants, although IMZ cells do not involute, they nevertheless progressively stop expressing CT and express postinvolution behaviors, including MIB-driven cell intercalation (resulting in CE) initiated in the form of the VAZ (Figure 1I, black, fusiform shapes), beginning at the midgastrula stage.
evidence: The introduction describes the transition in explants with reference to Figure 1I.

claim: In giant sandwich explants, the ends of the Vegetal Alignment Zone (VAZ) are unanchored, ending within the vegetal edge of the explant.
source: Here, in the explant, the ends of the VAZ are unanchored, ending within the vegetal edge of the explant (Figure 1I, asterisks) and when MIB-driven cell intercalation shortens the arc, it acts with CT in the more posterior portions of the IMZ to converge the IMZ medially.
evidence: The introduction describes the VAZ structure in explants with reference to Figure 1I.

claim: The posterior advance of mediolateral intercalation behavior marks the transition zone between the thick zone of continuing convergent thickening and the narrowing and extending zone of convergent extension.
source: The posterior advance of MIB (Figure 1J, black fusiform shapes flanked by asterisks) marks the transition zone between the thick zone of continuing CT and the narrowing and extending zone of CE, and corresponds to the point at which cells would be involuting in an intact embryo.
evidence: The introduction describes the transition zone with reference to Figure 1J.

claim: Ventralized Xenopus embryos close their blastopores in the absence of convergent extension.
source: These findings explain how ventralized Xenopus embryos (Scharf and Gerhart, 1980) and normal embryos of some amphibians such as Gastrotheca riobambae (del Pino, 1996) close their blastopores in the absence of CE (Keller and Shook, 2004; del Pino et al., 2007) and symmetrically, as are CT movements in normal Xenopus embryos.
evidence: The discussion cites previous studies showing ventralized embryos close their blastopores without CE.

claim: Normal embryos of Gastrotheca riobambae close their blastopores in the absence of convergent extension.
source: These findings explain how ventralized Xenopus embryos (Scharf and Gerhart, 1980) and normal embryos of some amphibians such as Gastrotheca riobambae (del Pino, 1996) close their blastopores in the absence of CE (Keller and Shook, 2004; del Pino et al., 2007) and symmetrically, as are CT movements in normal Xenopus embryos.
evidence: The discussion cites previous studies showing Gastrotheca riobambae embryos close their blastopores without CE.

claim: Convergent thickening generates all the IMZ convergence prior to the onset of convergent extension at the early midgastrula stage (stage 10.5, G+2hr).
source: Thus CT generates all the IMZ convergence prior to the onset of CE at the early midgastrula stage (stage 10.5, G+2hr).
evidence: The discussion concludes that CT generates all convergence before CE begins based on the results.

claim: Standard giant sandwich explants generate and maintain a consistent pattern of convergence force throughout gastrulation, neurulation, and into the tailbud stage.
source: Giant sandwich explants (IMZ and NIMZ) generate and maintain a consistent pattern of convergence force throughout gastrulation, neurulation, and into the tailbud stage.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the force generation pattern observed in the results.

claim: The IMZ can generate and maintain large, constant, convergence forces and transmit them over long distances for long periods.
source: We show that the IMZ can generate and maintain large, constant, convergence forces and transmit them over long distances for long periods.
evidence: The abstract summarizes a key finding of the study.

claim: Cells generate most or all of the force around the blastopore by convergent thickening until midgastrulation, when cells begin to progressively involute and generate force via the expression of mediolateral intercalation behavior.
source: We also demonstrate a previously unknown transition in which cells generate most or all of the force around the blastopore by CT until midgastrulation, when cells begin to progressively involute and generate force via the expression of MIB.
evidence: The abstract summarizes a key finding about the CT to MIB transition.

claim: The rate of convergence of giant sandwich explants peaked earlier than in whole embryos.
source: Time-lapse movies show that the mesodermal (IMZ) and neural (NIMZ) tissues in unencumbered (un-restrained) giant sandwich explants (e.g. Video 2) undergo convergence similar to that seen in embryos (e.g. Video 1), except that the rate peaked earlier in explants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and was only 57% of that in whole embryos during gastrulation (Table 1).
evidence: The results section describes the convergence rate in explants compared to embryos with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Table 1.

claim: The rate of convergence of giant sandwich explants was only 57% of that in whole embryos during gastrulation.
source: Time-lapse movies show that the mesodermal (IMZ) and neural (NIMZ) tissues in unencumbered (un-restrained) giant sandwich explants (e.g. Video 2) undergo convergence similar to that seen in embryos (e.g. Video 1), except that the rate peaked earlier in explants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and was only 57% of that in whole embryos during gastrulation (Table 1).
evidence: The results section describes the convergence rate in explants compared to embryos with reference to Table 1.

claim: Imaging explants as they were made revealed 600 %/hr convergence in the first three minutes after cutting.
source: Imaging explants as they were made revealed 600 %/hr convergence in the first three minutes after cutting (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), two orders of magnitude faster than that of post-construction explants or embryos (Table 1), suggesting that convergence against resisting tissues (e.g. the vegetal endoderm) resulted in stored elastic energy in the embryo, in line with prior findings (Beloussov et al., 1975; Beloussov, 1990; Fung, 1993).
evidence: The results section describes rapid convergence upon cutting with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Table 1.

claim: Rapid convergence upon cutting is two orders of magnitude faster than that of post-construction explants or embryos.
source: Imaging explants as they were made revealed 600 %/hr convergence in the first three minutes after cutting (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), two orders of magnitude faster than that of post-construction explants or embryos (Table 1), suggesting that convergence against resisting tissues (e.g. the vegetal endoderm) resulted in stored elastic energy in the embryo, in line with prior findings (Beloussov et al., 1975; Beloussov, 1990; Fung, 1993).
evidence: The results section compares convergence rates with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Table 1.

claim: Convergence against resisting tissues resulted in stored elastic energy in the embryo.
source: Imaging explants as they were made revealed 600 %/hr convergence in the first three minutes after cutting (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), two orders of magnitude faster than that of post-construction explants or embryos (Table 1), suggesting that convergence against resisting tissues (e.g. the vegetal endoderm) resulted in stored elastic energy in the embryo, in line with prior findings (Beloussov et al., 1975; Beloussov, 1990; Fung, 1993).
evidence: The results section infers stored elastic energy from rapid convergence upon cutting, citing previous studies.

claim: Unencumbered giants and intact embryos reached a minimal rate of convergence by 9 hr after the onset of gastrulation (G+9hr).
source: Unencumbered giants and intact embryos reached a minimal rate of convergence by 9 hr after the onset of gastrulation (G+9hr) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), when involution is complete and convergence occurs only as CE of the involuted mesodermal tissues and overlying neural tissue.
evidence: The results section describes the convergence rate over time with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At G+9hr, involution is complete and convergence occurs only as convergent extension of the involuted mesodermal tissues and overlying neural tissue.
source: Unencumbered giants and intact embryos reached a minimal rate of convergence by 9 hr after the onset of gastrulation (G+9hr) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), when involution is complete and convergence occurs only as CE of the involuted mesodermal tissues and overlying neural tissue.
evidence: The results section describes the developmental state at G+9hr.

claim: The dorsal tissues in giant sandwiches converged and extended well.
source: The dorsal tissues in giant sandwiches converged and extended well (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), and tissue differentiation was as expected from previous work, as assayed by markers for notochord and somitic mesoderm (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–H) (see Keller and Danilchik, 1988; Poznanski et al., 1997).
evidence: The results section describes tissue behavior in explants with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and 4.

claim: Tissue differentiation in giant sandwiches was as expected from previous work, as assayed by markers for notochord and somitic mesoderm.
source: The dorsal tissues in giant sandwiches converged and extended well (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), and tissue differentiation was as expected from previous work, as assayed by markers for notochord and somitic mesoderm (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–H) (see Keller and Danilchik, 1988; Poznanski et al., 1997).
evidence: The results section describes tissue differentiation with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and cites previous studies.

claim: Standard giant explants show a consistent pattern of circumblastoporal (mediolateral) tensile force increasing with time, in two major phases.
source: Assays of standard giant sandwich explants (Figure 2B), beginning between control stages 10.25 (G+1hr) and 11.5 (G+3.5hr), showed a consistent pattern of circumblastoporal (mediolateral) tensile force increasing with time, in two major phases (Figure 3A, blue and green lines), using either a stiffer probe (#3, spring constant = 27 μN/μm) or a less stiff probe (#4, spring constant = 12 μN/μm).
evidence: The results section describes the force pattern with reference to Figure 2B and Figure 3A.

claim: In the first phase of force increase, force increased steadily to over 1 μN by the end of gastrulation in control embryos (stage 13, G+6hr).
source: In the first phase, beginning when the explant pulled the cleat against the probe (Figure 2I), usually within the first 3 to 30 min of the assay, force increased steadily to over 1 μN by the end of gastrulation in control embryos (stage 13, G+6hr) and increased further by early neurulation (stage 14, G+7.5hr) when it plateaued at about 2 μN (Figure 3A, blue line).
evidence: The results section describes the first phase of force increase with reference to Figure 2I and Figure 3A.

claim: Force increased further by early neurulation (stage 14, G+7.5hr) when it plateaued at about 2 μN.
source: In the first phase, beginning when the explant pulled the cleat against the probe (Figure 2I), usually within the first 3 to 30 min of the assay, force increased steadily to over 1 μN by the end of gastrulation in control embryos (stage 13, G+6hr) and increased further by early neurulation (stage 14, G+7.5hr) when it plateaued at about 2 μN (Figure 3A, blue line).
evidence: The results section describes the plateau with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: A second phase of force increase began 3 hr later (late neurula stage 18, G+10.5hr) with most samples exhibiting a second plateau at about 4 to 5 μN by G+15 to 18.
source: A second phase of force increase began 3 hr later (late neurula stage 18, G+10.5hr) with most samples exhibiting a second plateau at about 4 to 5 μN by G+15 to 18 (Figure 3A, blue line; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section describes the second phase of force increase with reference to Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Animal cap sandwiches showed no convergence force.
source: Animal cap sandwiches, which do not normally converge or extend, showed no convergence force (Figure 3A, brown line; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), thus ruling out healing and other artifacts.
evidence: The results section describes animal cap controls with reference to Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining showed normal differentiation of somitic and notochordal tissues undergoing convergent extension in mechanically loaded (encumbered) sandwiches.
source: Immunohistochemical staining showed normal differentiation of somitic and notochordal tissues undergoing CE in mechanically loaded (encumbered) sandwiches (Appendix 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-H).
evidence: The results section describes tissue differentiation in loaded explants with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Tissues in each half of the sandwich were fused with their counterpart in the other half.
source: As in unencumbered sandwiches, tissues in each half of the sandwich were fused with their counterpart in the other half (see Keller and Danilchik, 1988; Poznanski et al., 1997).
evidence: The results section describes tissue fusion in sandwiches, citing previous studies.

claim: Notochords were sometimes split posteriorly in mechanically loaded sandwiches.
source: Notochords were sometimes split posteriorly (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C,G), perhaps related to retarded convergence compared to that of unencumbered giants (Figure 2—figure supplements 1B and 3).
evidence: The results section describes notochord splitting with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The NIMZ, especially the non-neural portion, converged very little in the tractor pull, as compared to unencumbered giants.
source: Also the NIMZ, especially the non-neural portion, converged very little in the tractor pull, as compared to unencumbered giants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and 3; Videos 2 and 4).
evidence: The results section describes NIMZ convergence with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and 3, and Videos 2 and 4.

claim: Giant explants express convergent thickening alone in early gastrula stages, followed by progressive transition to expression of mediolateral intercalation behavior/convergent extension.
source: Using standard giant explants, and dorsal, ventral, and ventralized explants allowed us to ferret out the relative contributions of CT and CE during the progressive transition from CT to CE. Giant explants express CT alone in early gastrula stages, followed by progressive transition to expression of MIB/CE.
evidence: The results section describes the CT to CE transition in giant explants.

claim: The IMZ of unencumbered giant explants converges equally across its mediolateral extent, without anisotropic (dorsally-biased) extension through G+2hr (stage 10.5).
source: The IMZ of unencumbered giant explants converges equally across its mediolateral extent, without anisotropic (dorsally-biased) extension through G+2hr (stage 10.5) (Figure 1G,H; Video 2, through about 13:34:57).
evidence: The results section describes convergence in unencumbered explants with reference to Figure 1G,H and Video 2.

claim: Convergent thickening is expressed early, from the onset of gastrulation, and everywhere in the IMZ.
source: Thus CT is expressed early, from the onset of gastrulation, and everywhere in the IMZ, rather than just ventrally and later, as previously thought (Keller and Danilchik, 1988).
evidence: The results section concludes that CT is expressed throughout the IMZ, citing a previous study.

claim: Tension appeared as early as stage 10 in early giant explants.
source: To measure early forces, giant explants were made from late blastulae (the future dorsal side identified by 'tipping and marking'; see Methods), mounted in the apparatus and measured before gastrulation began and prior to expression of MIB/CE. Tension appeared as early as stage 10 (Figure 3B, light blue line; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and rose to 0.3 μN of force prior to the onset of MIB, which occurs at G+2hr (Shih and Keller, 1992b; Lane and Keller, 1997), demonstrating that CT alone generates this early force.
evidence: The results section describes early force measurements with reference to Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Force rose to 0.3 μN prior to the onset of mediolateral intercalation behavior, which occurs at G+2hr.
source: Tension appeared as early as stage 10 (Figure 3B, light blue line; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and rose to 0.3 μN of force prior to the onset of MIB, which occurs at G+2hr (Shih and Keller, 1992b; Lane and Keller, 1997), demonstrating that CT alone generates this early force.
evidence: The results section describes early force measurements with reference to Figure 3B and cites previous studies.

claim: Convergent thickening alone generates early force prior to the onset of mediolateral intercalation behavior.
source: Tension appeared as early as stage 10 (Figure 3B, light blue line; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and rose to 0.3 μN of force prior to the onset of MIB, which occurs at G+2hr (Shih and Keller, 1992b; Lane and Keller, 1997), demonstrating that CT alone generates this early force.
evidence: The results section concludes that CT generates early force based on the timing of force appearance.

claim: Ventral 180° sandwich explants and explants of the entire marginal zone of UV ventralized embryos converge equally across their mediolateral extent until reaching an equilibrium state of convergence and thickening.
source: Ventral 180° sandwich explants (Figure 2D,E) and explants of the entire marginal zone of UV ventralized embryos (Figure 2F,G), both of which largely lack dorsal, CE expressing tissues (see Appendix 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 4M–P), converge equally across their mediolateral extent until reaching an equilibrium state of convergence and thickening (Video 3).
evidence: The results section describes convergence in ventral/ventralized explants with reference to Figure 2 and Video 3.

claim: Ventral sandwich explants showed initial force increase similar to standard giant explants and plateaued at about 2 μN.
source: These ventral sandwich explants showed initial force increase similar to standard giant explants and plateaued at about 2 μN, similar to standard giant explants, but neither exhibited the second phase of force production (Figure 3D, yellow, orange lines; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: The results section describes force generation in ventral explants with reference to Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ventral/ventralized explants did not exhibit the second phase of force production.
source: These ventral sandwich explants showed initial force increase similar to standard giant explants and plateaued at about 2 μN, similar to standard giant explants, but neither exhibited the second phase of force production (Figure 3D, yellow, orange lines; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: The results section describes force generation in ventral explants with reference to Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: During gastrulation, forces equivalent to those generated by a combination of convergent extension and convergent thickening in standard giants, are generated by convergent thickening alone in ventral/ventralized tissues.
source: These results show that during gastrulation, forces equivalent to those generated by a combination of CE and CT in standard giants, are generated by CT alone in ventral/ventralized tissues and that CT continues to operate if not replaced by CE.
evidence: The results section concludes that CT alone can generate forces equivalent to CT+CE based on ventral/ventralized explant data.

claim: Convergent thickening continues to operate if not replaced by convergent extension.
source: These results show that during gastrulation, forces equivalent to those generated by a combination of CE and CT in standard giants, are generated by CT alone in ventral/ventralized tissues and that CT continues to operate if not replaced by CE.
evidence: The results section concludes that CT persists in the absence of CE based on ventral/ventralized explant data.

claim: Late giant explants and Dorsal 180 explants show a more continuous increase of tensile force, with a moderate or no decline in the rate of force increase during the plateau of normal giants.
source: Late giant explants, made as giant sandwich explants (Figure 2A,B) but remain unencumbered until the late gastrula stage, and Dorsal 180 explants (Figure 2A,C), which develop largely dorsal tissues, show a more continuous increase of tensile force, with a moderate or no decline in the rate of force increase (Figure 3B and C, magenta and pink lines, respectively; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F) during the plateau of normal giants, and they show a final plateau of 3.5 to 4 μN (G+14hr; stage 21–22), a little lower and earlier than normal giant explants.
evidence: The results section describes force generation in late and dorsal explants with reference to Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Late giant explants and Dorsal 180 explants show a final plateau of 3.5 to 4 μN (G+14hr; stage 21–22), a little lower and earlier than normal giant explants.
source: Late giant explants, made as giant sandwich explants (Figure 2A,B) but remain unencumbered until the late gastrula stage, and Dorsal 180 explants (Figure 2A,C), which develop largely dorsal tissues, show a more continuous increase of tensile force, with a moderate or no decline in the rate of force increase (Figure 3B and C, magenta and pink lines, respectively; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F) during the plateau of normal giants, and they show a final plateau of 3.5 to 4 μN (G+14hr; stage 21–22), a little lower and earlier than normal giant explants.
evidence: The results section describes force generation in late and dorsal explants with reference to Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The more continuous rise in force in late and dorsal explants is correlated with absent or reduced ventral/ventrolateral regions lying between dorsal mediolateral intercalation behavior/convergent extension expressing tissue and the attachment strips.
source: This more continuous rise in force is correlated with absent or reduced ventral/ventrolateral regions lying between dorsal MIB/CE expressing tissue and the attachment strips, which suggests that the presence of ventrolateral (presumptive posterior) tissues accounts for the plateau.
evidence: The results section infers that the absence of ventrolateral tissues explains the lack of plateau.

claim: The presence of ventrolateral (presumptive posterior) tissues accounts for the plateau in standard giant explants.
source: This more continuous rise in force is correlated with absent or reduced ventral/ventrolateral regions lying between dorsal MIB/CE expressing tissue and the attachment strips, which suggests that the presence of ventrolateral (presumptive posterior) tissues accounts for the plateau.
evidence: The results section infers that ventrolateral tissues cause the plateau based on comparison of explant types.

claim: Unencumbered giants converge uniformly along their mediolateral axis at 10 %/hr.
source: Unencumbered giants converge (=negative strain) uniformly along their mediolateral axis (data not shown; see Video 2) at 10 %/hr (Table 1), whereas encumbered giants converge at 70% of this rate in the dorsal sectors that are expressing CE, but there is no convergence in the more ventrolateral sectors not yet expressing CE during the first phase of force increase (Table 1; Video 4).
evidence: The results section describes convergence rates with reference to Table 1 and Video 2.

claim: Encumbered giants converge at 70% of the rate of unencumbered giants in the dorsal sectors that are expressing convergent extension.
source: Unencumbered giants converge (=negative strain) uniformly along their mediolateral axis (data not shown; see Video 2) at 10 %/hr (Table 1), whereas encumbered giants converge at 70% of this rate in the dorsal sectors that are expressing CE, but there is no convergence in the more ventrolateral sectors not yet expressing CE during the first phase of force increase (Table 1; Video 4).
evidence: The results section describes convergence rates with reference to Table 1 and Video 4.

claim: There is no convergence in the more ventrolateral sectors not yet expressing convergent extension during the first phase of force increase in encumbered giants.
source: Unencumbered giants converge (=negative strain) uniformly along their mediolateral axis (data not shown; see Video 2) at 10 %/hr (Table 1), whereas encumbered giants converge at 70% of this rate in the dorsal sectors that are expressing CE, but there is no convergence in the more ventrolateral sectors not yet expressing CE during the first phase of force increase (Table 1; Video 4).
evidence: The results section describes regional differences in convergence with reference to Table 1 and Video 4.

claim: Shear accounted for substantially more of explant convergence than did sled movement.
source: Comparison of the rate of shear of the explant with respect to the attachment strips (the rate of convergence of the edges of the widest part of the IMZ minus the convergence of the sled toward the anchor (Appendix 3)), showed that shear accounted for substantially more of explant convergence than did sled movement (Table 1).
evidence: The results section describes the contribution of shear to convergence with reference to Table 1.

claim: During the plateau, overall IMZ convergence dropped by 1.6 %/hr for probe three while shear dropped by 1.2 %/hr, such that it matched the remaining convergence of 2.5 %/hr.
source: During the plateau, overall IMZ convergence dropped by 1.6 %/hr for probe three while shear dropped by 1.2 %/hr, such that it matched the remaining convergence of 2.5 %/hr (Table 1; Appendix 3).
evidence: The results section describes changes during the plateau with reference to Table 1.

claim: The overall decline in convergence during the plateau was explained by a 0.6 %/hr increase in strain in ventrolateral tissues and a 0.2 %/hr decline in convergence in dorsal tissues.
source: By region, the overall decline in convergence was explained by a 0.6 %/hr increase in strain in ventrolateral tissues and a 0.2 %/hr decline in convergence in dorsal tissues.
evidence: The results section describes regional changes during the plateau.

claim: The plateau is due primarily to the increased strain of the ventrolateral tissues.
source: Thus, the plateau is due primarily to the increased strain of the ventrolateral tissues; this could be explained either by a decline in stiffness, or by a decline or stall of force generation in this region.
evidence: The results section concludes that ventrolateral tissue strain causes the plateau.

claim: The end of the plateau in giant explant assays is associated with significantly increased convergence of the ventrolateral regions by 2.2 %/hr and significantly decreased convergence by 1.5 %/hr in dorsal regions.
source: Also, the end of the plateau in giant explant assays is associated with significantly increased convergence of the ventrolateral regions by 2.2 %/hr and significantly decreased convergence by 1.5 %/hr in dorsal regions (Table 1), suggesting an increase in stiffness or force generation in these ventrolateral regions contributes to the end of the plateau.
evidence: The results section describes changes at the end of the plateau with reference to Table 1.

claim: An increase in stiffness or force generation in ventrolateral regions contributes to the end of the plateau.
source: Also, the end of the plateau in giant explant assays is associated with significantly increased convergence of the ventrolateral regions by 2.2 %/hr and significantly decreased convergence by 1.5 %/hr in dorsal regions (Table 1), suggesting an increase in stiffness or force generation in these ventrolateral regions contributes to the end of the plateau.
evidence: The results section infers that changes in ventrolateral tissue properties end the plateau.

claim: Applying additional exogenous tension to an explant prevents further force generation by the explant until shear has allowed enough convergence such that the instantaneous stall force rises above the current level of tension.
source: Our model above, that encumbered explants are increasing tensile force as they recruit more cells into MIB, predicts that applying additional exogenous tension to an explant should prevent further force generation by the explant until shear has allowed enough convergence such that the instantaneous stall force rises above the current level of tension. To test this, we applied additional tension to explants at various stages through the end of the plateau, by increasing the strain on them (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–E). Explants (n = 9) generally showed an immediate 0.5 to 0.6 μN increase in tension, which decayed quickly over the next 15 to 30 min, then remained static until the explant's projected rise in force prior to being strained reached its new, current level of tension (e.g. Figure 3—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: The results section describes experiments testing the stall force model with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Explants subjected to increased tension showed an immediate 0.5 to 0.6 μN increase in tension, which decayed quickly over the next 15 to 30 min, then remained static until the explant's projected rise in force prior to being strained reached its new, current level of tension.
source: Explants (n = 9) generally showed an immediate 0.5 to 0.6 μN increase in tension, which decayed quickly over the next 15 to 30 min, then remained static until the explant's projected rise in force prior to being strained reached its new, current level of tension (e.g. Figure 3—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: The results section describes the response to increased tension with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Tensioned explants did not produce higher final amounts, or rates of increase, of force.
source: In no case did tensioned explants produce higher final amounts, or rates of increase, of force.
evidence: The results section describes the outcome of tension experiments.

claim: Increased tension stalls the force increase in explants.
source: These results demonstrate that increased tension stalls the force increase, as predicted, and that while the explant can sustain greater tension, increased tension alone does not trigger increased force production.
evidence: The results section concludes that increased tension stalls force increase based on experimental results.

claim: While the explant can sustain greater tension, increased tension alone does not trigger increased force production.
source: These results demonstrate that increased tension stalls the force increase, as predicted, and that while the explant can sustain greater tension, increased tension alone does not trigger increased force production.
evidence: The results section concludes that tension does not trigger force production based on experimental results.

claim: Reducing strain by moving the anchor toward the probe resulted in an immediate observed relaxation across the explant of from 0.6 to 1.2 μN.
source: Reducing strain by moving the anchor toward the probe (Figure 3—figure supplement 4F–I) enough to decrease tension on the explant by 1.2 to 1.4 μN resulted in an immediate observed relaxation across the explant of from 0.6 to 1.2 μN, with the remainder corresponding to the rapid recoil of elastic strain during anchor movement (<1 s).
evidence: The results section describes the response to reduced tension with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: After the initial, rapid elastic recoil, explants converged at a rate similar to unencumbered explants (about 10 %/hr) until recovering their prior tension levels.
source: After the initial, rapid elastic recoil, explants converged at a rate similar to unencumbered explants (about 10 %/hr, see Table 1), until recovering their prior tension levels (e.g. Figure 3—figure supplement 4F,G).
evidence: The results section describes convergence after tension reduction with reference to Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Recovery of tension was consistently rapid (<15 min) during the first phase of force increase.
source: Recovery was consistently (n = 6) rapid (<15 min) during the first phase of force increase, whereas it was consistently (n = 4) slower (30 min or more) during the major plateau or during dorsal bottle cell re-expansion.
evidence: The results section describes the rate of tension recovery.

claim: Recovery of tension was consistently slower (30 min or more) during the major plateau or during dorsal bottle cell re-expansion.
source: Recovery was consistently (n = 6) rapid (<15 min) during the first phase of force increase, whereas it was consistently (n = 4) slower (30 min or more) during the major plateau or during dorsal bottle cell re-expansion.
evidence: The results section describes the rate of tension recovery.

claim: After recovery during the first phase of force increase, explants converged at rates more typical of encumbered explants (about 4 %/hr).
source: After recovery during the first phase of force increase, explants converged at rates more typical of encumbered explants (about 4 %/hr, Table 1).
evidence: The results section describes convergence rates after tension recovery with reference to Table 1.

claim: Rapid recovery of tension supports the model that explants generate increasing tension until reaching an instantaneous stall force, with consequently retarded convergence during all but their initial period of force increase.
source: This rapid recovery supports our model that explants generate increasing tension until reaching an instantaneous stall force, with consequently retarded convergence during all but their initial period of force increase.
evidence: The results section interprets the rapid recovery as supporting the stall force model.

claim: The slower recovery of the explants to normal levels of tension during the plateau is consistent with lower levels of stored elastic energy across the explant as a whole at this time.
source: The slower recovery of the explants to normal levels of tension during the plateau is consistent with lower levels of stored elastic energy, across the explant as a whole at this time (Discussion).
evidence: The results section interprets the slower recovery as indicating lower stored elastic energy.

claim: The fractional recoil was 41% during the first phase of force production, compared to 28% during the plateau.
source: We found that the fractional recoil was 41% (S.E. =±5%, n = 6) during the first phase of force production, compared to 28% (S.E. = ±5%, n = 3) during the plateau.
evidence: The results section reports measured fractional recoil values.

claim: The recoil rate was 670 %/hr during the first phase of force increase, compared to 390 %/hr during the plateau.
source: The recoil rate was 670 %/hr (S.E. = ±90 %/hr; n = 7) during the first phase of force increase (similar to the recoil rate of 600 %/hr seen in explants freshly cut from intact early gastrulae), compared to 390 %/hr (S.E. = ±32 %/hr; n = 3) during the plateau.
evidence: The results section reports measured recoil rate values.

claim: During a tractor pull, explants store considerable elastic strain-energy, more of which is recoverable during the first phase of force increase than during the subsequent plateau.
source: These results show that during a tractor pull, explants, like the intact embryo, store considerable elastic strain-energy, more of which is recoverable during the first phase of force increase than during the subsequent plateau.
evidence: The results section concludes that explants store elastic energy based on recoil measurements.

claim: The difference in recoverable elastic energy is consistent with the idea that ventrolateral tissues have reduced force accumulation during the plateau.
source: This is consistent with the idea that ventrolateral tissues have reduced force accumulation during the plateau (Discussion).
evidence: The results section interprets the elastic energy data as consistent with reduced force in ventrolateral tissues.

claim: The modulus estimated from structural stiffness along the mediolateral axis of giant explants rose significantly from 14 Pa at late gastrulation (G+4.8hr) to 21 Pa by mid neurulation (G+8.7hr).
source: The modulus estimated from structural stiffness's along the mediolateral axis of giant explants rose significantly from 14 Pa (Pascals) at late gastrulation (G+4.8hr) to 21 Pa by mid neurulation (G+8.7hr) (p<0.01, paired t-test, n = 6 vs. 6) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The results section reports measured stiffness values with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: After release from tension, explants recoil rapidly and typically returned to near their initial width within three minutes, with about 25% of the initially applied strain lost to permanent, or plastic, deformation.
source: After release from tension, explants recoil rapidly and typically returned to near their initial width within three minutes, with about 25% of the initially applied strain lost to permanent, or plastic, deformation, leaving them about 3% longer, indicating that while they can store elastic strain energy, some dissipation occurs, for example by the rearrangement of cells or structural elements within them.
evidence: The results section describes the recoil behavior after tension release.

claim: D180° and V180° sandwich explants showed a trend of increasing stiffness from gastrula to neurula stages.
source: D180° and V180° sandwich explants also showed a trend of increasing stiffness from gastrula to neurula stages (Figure 5B) with both showing an increase between stages 12 and 14 (G+4.3 and 7.6hr) but showed no significant differences from each other at any stage.
evidence: The results section describes stiffness trends with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: D180° and V180° sandwich explants showed no significant differences in stiffness from each other at any stage.
source: D180° and V180° sandwich explants also showed a trend of increasing stiffness from gastrula to neurula stages (Figure 5B) with both showing an increase between stages 12 and 14 (G+4.3 and 7.6hr) but showed no significant differences from each other at any stage.
evidence: The results section reports no significant difference in stiffness between explant types.

claim: Presumptive ectodermal (AC) sandwiches showed increased structural stiffness from gastrula to neurula stages.
source: Presumptive ectodermal (AC) sandwiches strained an average of 24% over 180 s showed increased structural stiffness (p<0.01, n = 5 vs. 3) from gastrula to neurula stages (Figure 5B), but their stiffness is not significantly different from that of standard giants at either stage.
evidence: The results section reports stiffness measurements for AC sandwiches with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: AC explants showed plastic deformations of 25% of total strain by late neurulation.
source: By late neurulation AC explants also showed plastic deformations of 25% of total strain.
evidence: The results section reports plastic deformation in AC explants.

claim: AC explants were substantially more plastic during gastrulation, with about 65% of the total strain remaining as plastic deformation.
source: AC explants were substantially more plastic during gastrulation however, with about 65% of the total strain remaining as plastic deformation, suggesting a lesser ability to store elastic strain energy than during neurulation.
evidence: The results section reports plastic deformation in AC explants during gastrulation.

claim: All explant types measured exhibit similar structural stiffness, and their stiffness increases by about the same amount from gastrulation to neurulation.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, all explants types measured, although comprised of different sets of tissues, exhibit similar structural stiffness, and their stiffness increases by about the same amount from gastrulation to neurulation.
evidence: The results section summarizes the stiffness findings across explant types.

claim: Standard giants, D180°, V180° and AC explants all showed a trend of increasing spring stiffness between gastrula and neurula stages.
source: Standard giants, D180°, V180° and AC explants all showed a trend of increasing spring stiffness between gastrula and neurula stages (Figure 5C).
evidence: The results section describes spring stiffness trends with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Standard giants did not differ significantly in spring stiffness between gastrula stages but increased significantly from stage to stage thereafter, doubling between G+4.8 and G+8.7.
source: Standard giants did not differ significantly between gastrula stages but increased significantly from stage to stage thereafter (p<0.01, n's = 6 vs. 6; 6 vs. 3), doubling between G+4.8 and G+8.7.
evidence: The results section reports spring stiffness changes in standard giants.

claim: AC sandwich explants increased significantly in spring stiffness between gastrula and neurula stages.
source: AC sandwich explants also increased significantly (p<0.05, n = 3 vs. 3) between gastrula and neurula stages.
evidence: The results section reports spring stiffness changes in AC explants.

claim: Standard giants had significantly higher spring stiffness than AC sandwich explants by 5 to 6 fold at all stages.
source: Standard giants had significantly higher spring stiffness than AC sandwich explants by 5 to 6 fold at all stages (p<0.05 during gastrulation, p<0.01 during neurulation; n's = 3 vs. 3 to 6), indicating that ectodermal tissues contribute little to the ability of the IMZ to resist tension along the mediolateral axis during tractor pulls.
evidence: The results section reports differences in spring stiffness between explant types.

claim: Ectodermal tissues contribute little to the ability of the IMZ to resist tension along the mediolateral axis during tractor pulls.
source: Standard giants had significantly higher spring stiffness than AC sandwich explants by 5 to 6 fold at all stages (p<0.05 during gastrulation, p<0.01 during neurulation; n's = 3 vs. 3 to 6), indicating that ectodermal tissues contribute little to the ability of the IMZ to resist tension along the mediolateral axis during tractor pulls.
evidence: The results section infers the contribution of ectodermal tissues based on spring stiffness comparisons.

claim: V180° explants were similar in spring stiffness to standard giants until after mid-neurulation when their spring stiffness was moderately (37%) but significantly lower.
source: V180° explants were similar to standard giants until after mid-neurulation when their spring stiffness was moderately (37%) but significantly lower (p<0.01, n = 2 vs. 3).
evidence: The results section reports spring stiffness differences between V180° and standard giants.

claim: The greater spring stiffness of giants vs. ventral 180° explants by the end of neurulation is consistent with increased overall spring stiffness of giants as dorsal tissue differentiation progresses laterally.
source: The greater spring stiffness of giants vs. ventral 180° explants by the end of neurulation is consistent with increased overall spring stiffness of giants as dorsal tissue differentiation progresses laterally.
evidence: The results section interprets the spring stiffness difference as related to tissue differentiation.

claim: In the context of sandwich explants by the time of the plateau, ventrolateral tissues undergo more strain than dorsal tissues, because dorsal tissues have a larger and increasing sectional area.
source: In the context of our sandwich explants by the time of the plateau, ventrolateral tissues undergo more strain than dorsal tissues, because dorsal tissues have a larger and increasing sectional area.
evidence: The results section explains differential strain based on sectional area differences.

claim: The mean mediolateral tensile force per cell rises during the first half of gastrulation and stabilizes by mid gastrulation at around 2.3 nN/cell.
source: We estimate that the mean mediolateral tensile force per cell rises during the first half of gastrulation and stabilizes by mid gastrulation at around 2.3 nN/cell, where it remains (Table 2).
evidence: The results section reports estimated force per cell with reference to Table 2.

claim: The constant force per cell is consistent with the idea that increasing stage-specific maximal force generation is limited primarily by morphogenesis, as it increases the sagittal sectional area.
source: The constant force per cell is consistent with the idea that increasing stage-specific maximal force generation is limited primarily by morphogenesis, as it increases the SSA.
evidence: The results section interprets the constant force per cell as indicating morphogenesis limits force increase.

claim: Tensional stress within the effective sagittal sectional area was roughly 4-fold lower than the mediolateral tensile stress estimated from extension forces exerted by dorsal tissues in a gel.
source: We also calculated tensional stress within the effective SSA (Table 2), which was roughly 4-fold lower than the mediolateral tensile stress estimated from extension forces exerted by dorsal tissues in a gel (Zhou et al., 2015), which is not surprising given that their measurements capture all of the force generated during late neurula stages in tissue that has undergone normal morphogenesis, compared to our which primarily capture forces generated around the blastopore, as described above.
evidence: The results section compares tensional stress to previous measurements, citing Zhou et al., 2015.

claim: Xenopus embryonic tissues stiffen about two fold along their mediolateral axis around the end of gastrulation, regardless of the tissue type.
source: Xenopus embryonic tissues stiffen about two fold along their mediolateral axis around the end of gastrulation, regardless of the tissue type, suggesting a systemic mechanism.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the stiffening observation and suggests a systemic mechanism.

claim: The increase in the stiffness of all the tissues at the end of gastrulation may cause decreased plasticity, as well as the resetting of pseudo-elasticity to a thinner epithelial set point.
source: Whatever the causes, the increase in the stiffness of all the tissues at the end of gastrulation may cause decreased plasticity, as well as the resetting of pseudo-elasticity to a thinner epithelial set point (Luu et al., 2011).
evidence: The discussion speculates about the consequences of tissue stiffening, citing Luu et al., 2011.

claim: Previous estimates of AP compressive stiffness of dorsal isolates at stage 11.5 are very similar to ML tensile structural stiffness at stage 11.5 measured in this study.
source: Previous estimates of AP compressive stiffness of dorsal isolates at stage 11.5 (about 14 Pascals, Moore et al., 1995a; Zhou et al., 2009), are very similar to ML tensile structural stiffness at stage 11.5 (G+3.5hr) measured here (Figure 5B), suggesting that the same mechanical elements may be resisting ML widening in both cases.
evidence: The discussion compares current measurements to previous studies, citing Moore et al., 1995a and Zhou et al., 2009.

claim: The same mechanical elements may be resisting ML widening in both AP compression and ML tension tests.
source: Previous estimates of AP compressive stiffness of dorsal isolates at stage 11.5 (about 14 Pascals, Moore et al., 1995a; Zhou et al., 2009), are very similar to ML tensile structural stiffness at stage 11.5 (G+3.5hr) measured here (Figure 5B), suggesting that the same mechanical elements may be resisting ML widening in both cases.
evidence: The discussion infers that similar mechanical elements are involved based on similar stiffness values.

claim: The observed transmission of forces across the full length of the IMZ makes it clear that tissue stiffness links the entire embryo into a mechanical 'mechanome'.
source: In any case, the observed transmission of forces across the full length of the IMZ makes it clear that tissue stiffness links the entire embryo into a mechanical 'mechanome' (Kamm, 2006; Lang, 2007) in which major regional morphogenic movements can affect one another.
evidence: The discussion concludes that force transmission links the embryo mechanically, citing Kamm, 2006 and Lang, 2007.

claim: Major regional morphogenic movements can affect one another mechanically in the embryo.
source: In any case, the observed transmission of forces across the full length of the IMZ makes it clear that tissue stiffness links the entire embryo into a mechanical 'mechanome' (Kamm, 2006; Lang, 2007) in which major regional morphogenic movements can affect one another.
evidence: The discussion concludes that regional movements can affect each other based on force transmission.

claim: Molecular interdictions of epiboly of the animal cap can affect blastopore closure on the other pole of the embryo.
source: This accounts for the fact that molecular interdictions of epiboly of the animal cap can affect blastopore closure on the other pole of the embryo, although no molecular perturbation was made there, and that the blastopore closure defect can be rescued by cutting off the animal cap, thus breaking the mechanical link (e.g. Eagleson et al., 2015).
evidence: The discussion cites an example of mechanical linkage affecting morphogenesis, citing Eagleson et al., 2015.

claim: The blastopore closure defect caused by animal cap epiboly disruption can be rescued by cutting off the animal cap, thus breaking the mechanical link.
source: This accounts for the fact that molecular interdictions of epiboly of the animal cap can affect blastopore closure on the other pole of the embryo, although no molecular perturbation was made there, and that the blastopore closure defect can be rescued by cutting off the animal cap, thus breaking the mechanical link (e.g. Eagleson et al., 2015).
evidence: The discussion cites an example of mechanical linkage affecting morphogenesis, citing Eagleson et al., 2015.
